rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Start of Round 2.1 Card Deal 2.2 Turn 2.2.1 Ordinary combinations 2.2.2 Special combinations 2.3 Round End 2.4 Game End 3 Options Overview The player who finishes playing their hand first in a round wins that round, and immediately wins when they win 3 rounds. [ Fast tutorial ] Start of Round The player with the lowest score starts the round. If tied, the player who went first least recently starts. Card Deal The deck contains 4 copies each of 1-9 plus four Crisps. Each player then receives 12 cards. 4 Cards are removed from the round blind. Turn There are 4 ordinary and 2 special sets/run: Ordinary combinations - Single - Pair - Run of Singles (minimum 3) - Run of Pairs (minimum 2 pairs / 4 cards) Special combinations - Three of a kind - Four of a kind A Crisp CANNOT be used in a Run. The first player can play any type they wish. The remaining players either follow or pass, this continues until someone passes or someone empties their hand. If you Follow with an Ordinary, it must be the same type of Ordinary, it must be the same Length of Ordinary, it must be equal or higher rank. If you Follow with a Special, the previous play MUST contain a Crisp, otherwise you have to Follow with Ordinary. In addition, a Special may follow a Special if either it contains more cards OR the same quantity but a higher rank. Round End If the round ends with someone passing, the player just before them can either take the faceup card set aside at the start or a blind deck card, after which the passing player has to take the card from the other option. If the round ends with someone emptying their hand, they score 1 point. If Game End isn't triggered, start a new round. Game End The game ends as soon as a player scores 3 points. Options - No face-up draw : After someone passes, both players draw a card from the deck face-down. - Special rank runs : Crisps can be used in runs. - Automatic turn skip : The game checks only public information to determine whether a player has any chance of beating the current combination regardless of the cards in hand. If all relevant higher cards are discarded already, the turn is skipped automatically.

[Rating: 1/10] Two-player trick taking games so rarely work or feel natural and this one is no exception. Melds too restrictive and the limited use case of the "C" card only muddles things further. Having to draw a card and force your opponent to take the other can create an interesting decision point but also introduces a sliver of luck that can be difficult to mitigate.

[Rating: 2/10] It's kinda fun to play, but only in the way that playing cards in general can be fun. It's a weird kitchen sink design that wants to be a trick-taker, ladder-climbing, hand management game where you're playing what essentially amount to poker hands. So... because it steals a bunch of ideas that are inherently fun from well-designed games, it can feel fun in the moment, but none of it comes together in a thoughtful, cohesive, or balanced way. The leader almost always wins if they're playing smartly as the follower doesn't have any way of countering bad draws or strategically following / passing

[Rating: 4/10] Much better ladder games out there than this one...depending on people's hands you could be passing almost every trick played in a round. It's also quite light so quite possibly not in my wheelhouse.

[Rating: 5/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  It works. I'm not a huge fan of two player card games in most instances, and I'd still be picking Claim or Fox in the Forest over this one even though I realize this one is a two player ladder game.

[Rating: 5/10] Thought I would like this since I've been enjoying Scout so much. Didn't do much for me.

[Rating: 5/10] Simple pvp ladder climbing game. Felt like there is one strategy to win and you needed to execute that strategy only in order to win. No theme and pretty bland.

[Rating: 5/10] There are tens or hundreds of trick taking games. This one has nothing special and is limited to 2 players, so while it's fun enough to play, I can't consider it a great game.

[Rating: 5/10] I've tried it now. I prefer Haggis in the "normal deck ladder shedder" and Ptolemy or Dickory if it has to be the "draw more cards" sub family. It sounds so dumb after a board game day were I played several of my very faves, Crisps was the most fun, that I'm still giving it a low grade but it's because while I LOVE ladder shedders, I don't need a bunch of similar variants. So far Dalmuti is my fave at 4+, Dickory at two, Haggis at three, Ptolemy as a fun-for-variety at two, and that leaves Bacon and Crisps at the wayside as too-similar-but-slightly-worse.
